notes:
## Large language model
A large language model (LLM) is a machine learning model (typically a neural network) trained on a vast amount of text for natural language processing tasks, especially language generation. LLMs can typically generate, summarize, translate, and analyze text in many contexts. They are the basis for many modern chatbots, such as ChatGPT, Claude, Vibe, Gemini, Grok, Qwen, DeepSeek and writing assistants such as Grammarly.
LLMs are typically based on the transformer neural network architecture. Generative pre-trained transformers (GPTs) are a type of LLM that is pre-trained to predict the next word. GPTs are then often fine-tuned to follow instructions and to behave as assistants.
Biased or inaccurate training data can make an LLM's output less reliable. A software harness can provide LLMs with memory and access to tools such as web search. Benchmark evaluations for LLMs attempt to measure model reasoning, factual accuracy, alignment, and safety.

plan.title: How ChatGPT Works: Predicting the Next Word
plan.description: Large language models like ChatGPT are neural networks trained on vast amounts of text to predict the next word. This video explains how that one simple skill becomes a helpful assistant, and where it can fail.

beats.narration: You type a question, and a fluent answer appears in seconds. But under the hood, the machine is doing something surprisingly simple. It is guessing the next word, over and over.

props.title: How does ChatGPT actually work?
props.subtitle: One simple trick behind a very smart-seeming machine

beats.narration: Think of the autocomplete on your phone. You type "see you" and it suggests "soon." A large language model is that idea, scaled up enormously.
A large language model, or LLM, is a neural network trained on a vast amount of text. Its main job is language generation.

props.definition: A machine learning model, typically a neural network, trained on a vast amount of text for language tasks, especially generating text.

beats.narration: Because of that training, it can generate, summarize, translate, and analyze text in many contexts. One skill, many uses.
So how does it learn? First, it reads huge amounts of text. Then it is trained to predict the next word. Then it is adjusted to follow instructions.
Each wrong guess nudges the network's internal settings a little. After countless guesses, it gets very good at patterns in language: grammar, facts, and style.
Most of these models are built on the transformer architecture. That design helps the network weigh which earlier words matter most for the next one.

props.text: Transformers help a model weigh which earlier words matter most.

beats.narration: That is what GPT stands for. Generative: it produces text. Pre-trained: it learns from vast text first. Transformer: the architecture underneath.

props.heading: What GPT means
items: Pre-trained: it learns from vast text first

beats.narration: A model that only predicts the next word is not yet a helpful assistant. So it is fine-tuned to follow instructions and behave like one.
It then writes its answer one word at a time. Each new word is added to the text, and the model predicts again, until the answer is done.

props.title: It then writes its answer one word at a

beats.narration: Add a software harness and it gets more. A harness can give the model memory, and tools like web search. That is how chatbots do more than guess.
But there is a catch. Biased or inaccurate training data can make the output less reliable. The model learns patterns, and it can repeat the mistakes in them.
That is why researchers use benchmarks. They try to measure reasoning, factual accuracy, alignment, and safety, so we know how far to trust a model.
So the big idea is simple. A large language model learns patterns from vast text, then predicts the next word, again and again. Enjoy it, but check the facts.

props.text: An LLM predicts the next word, again and again, so check its facts.
